title: Ratnakara asks his family
hook: a robber asks his family to share his sin, and Patanjali's sutra on turning a harmful thought around
carry: see where harm ends, then cultivate its opposite
tomorrow: Who is Ishvara in the Yoga Sutra?

segments.voice: Yesterday in Yoga: abhyasa and vairagya, practice and letting go, hold a mind as restless as the wind.
screen: `PRACTICE AND LETTING GO.` · `AS HARD TO HOLD AS THE WIND.`

segments.voice: Before he was the poet of the Ramayana, a well-loved later story says, Valmiki was a highway robber named Ratnakara. He stopped travelers in the forest and took what they had, to feed his family. One day he stops a sage, Narada in many tellings, who isn't afraid. The sage asks one question. Your family eats from this. Will they share the sin of it too? Go and ask. Ratnakara goes home and asks. Every one of them says no. The food is ours. The deed is yours.
screen: `A ROBBER IN THE FOREST.` → `WILL THEY SHARE THE SIN?` → `THE DEED IS YOURS.`

segments.voice: Ratnakara follows his harm to where it ends, and it ends with him alone. So he turns. He sits chanting Rama's name so long, the story goes, that an anthill rises over him, valmika, and he comes out as Valmiki. Patanjali puts that same turn into a sutra. Just after the restraints, beginning with ahimsa, non-harm, and the observances, he says, in paraphrase: when thoughts that pull against these trouble you, cultivate the opposite. Pratipaksha bhavana. The next sutra takes the harmful thought apart. It may be done by you, done through someone else, or just approved of. It may come from greed, anger or confusion. It may be mild, middling or intense. Whichever it is, it ends in endless pain and not knowing. Seeing that, cultivate the opposite. So this isn't, think happy thoughts. You follow the thought honestly to where it leads, the way Ratnakara walked home and asked. Many teachers read the story that way. Vyasa's commentary pictures someone tempted to harm remembering why they took up yoga at all. That's the week: a seed, a dancer, a prince, a serpent, a wind. Now a storm, and Yoga's answer. Not fight it, not obey it. Turn it around.
screen: `RATNAKARA BECOMES VALMIKI.` · `CULTIVATE THE OPPOSITE.` · `GREED, ANGER, CONFUSION.` · `FOLLOW IT TO WHERE IT ENDS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one small, recent irritation, nothing raw, and let the sharp thought arrive. Without scolding it, follow it a few steps ahead, if I said it, then what, and notice the cost; then let its other side come up, patience, fairness or simple quiet, and rest there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold the person you were annoyed with in prayer.
Yoga. In Patanjali's sutras, when a thought against non-harm arrives, yoga means seeing where it ends and cultivating its opposite, pratipaksha bhavana.
Your line: see where harm ends, then cultivate its opposite. Ratnakara asked, and turned. Same time tomorrow.

howItsDone: In the Yoga Sutras, the counsel to cultivate the opposite sits right after the restraints, such as non-harm, and the observances; students of Yoga philosophy practice it in reflection and in the moment a harmful thought arises, and the robber who became Valmiki is a story Hindu families tell children about owning what you do.

Ratnakara.meaning: the robber who, in later tellings, became the poet Valmiki

ahimsa.meaning: non-harm, the first of Patanjali's restraints

sources.ref: Yoga Sutras 2.33 (when troubled by contrary thoughts, cultivate the opposite)
Yoga Sutras 2.34 (harmful thoughts done, caused or approved; from greed, anger or delusion; mild, middling or intense; ending in endless pain and ignorance)
Vyasa, Yoga Bhashya on 2.33 (the practitioner tempted to harm recalls the refuge of yoga)

Ratnakara/Valmiki legend (the robber asks his family to share his sin; chanting Rama's name; the anthill), in later tellings, not in Valmiki's Ramayana itself: the Adhyatma Ramayana tells it with seven sages; popular retellings name him Ratnakara and the sage Narada
